findings.text: I read: the main lines run through both testaments without a break. The NT quotes the OT on three of them. It repeats the words of two more without a formula (Psa 37:11 / Mat 5:5; and Pro 25:7 / Luk 14:10 in substance).

In the OT readings, humbling is overwhelmingly before God: In all 20 verses of batch 1 group I it is done before God, or in answer to his word, by the verse or its passage; Humility toward another person is thin. It appears in Pro 25:6–7 (the seat), Pro 16:19 ("a lowly spirit with the poor"), Num 12:3 (Moses meek when spoken against), 2Sa 6:22 (David abased in Michal's eyes) and Gen 16:9 (Hagar told to submit).

In the NT readings, three groups are about how one stands toward others: humility toward one another (batch 4 III, 7), gentleness in meeting others (batch 4 IV, 11), and submission among people (batch 5 II, 20). That is 38 of the 77 NT verses: "in humility count others more significant than yourselves" (Phili 2:3); "Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another" (1Pe 5:5); "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" (Eph 5:21).

In the OT accounts, those who humble themselves are mostly kings and the people, in the narrative of 2 Chronicles and Kings: Rehoboam and the princes, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Josiah, and those who did not (Amon, Zedekiah, Belshazzar, Pharaoh): What follows is national and measured: wrath turned "so as not to make a complete destruction" (2Ch 12:12), and disaster delayed to "his son's days" (1Ki 21:29).

In the NT the one who humbles himself is any person. What follows is named as: "justified" (Luk 18:14); "grace" (Jam 4:6); "exalt you … at the proper time" (1Pe 5:6); "rest for your souls" (Mat 11:29).
The NT has a submission verb, hypotassō, 32 verses read. It is used of submitting to God (Jam 4:7; Heb 12:9) and among people.
The OT verses read have nothing of that range. The nearest are Gen 16:9 ("submit to her"), Psa 81:11 ("Israel would not submit to me") and 2Ch 30:8 ("yield yourselves to the Lord").

The NT counterparts read are acts: the tax collector who "beat his breast" (Luk 18:13); "Be wretched and mourn and weep" before "Humble yourselves" (Jam 4:9–10); Paul humbled before the unrepentant, to "mourn over many" (2Cor 12:21).
In the OT the ground for humbling is God himself and his word: "The Lord is righteous" (2Ch 12:6); "when you heard" (2Ki 22:19); "trembles at my word" (Isa 66:2).

In the NT a new ground is named: Christ, and Christ's own way: "Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus" (Phili 2:5); "Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example" (1Pe 2:21); "out of reverence for Christ" (Eph 5:21); "by the meekness and gentleness of Christ" (2Cor 10:1); "learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29).

The source named also changes. Gentleness is "the fruit of the Spirit" (Gal 5:22–23), and the mind of the flesh "does not submit … indeed, it cannot" (Rom 8:7). The OT verses read name God reviving the lowly (Isa 57:15) and the heart being humbled (Lev 26:41). They do not name an inner source given for it.

He teaches it: He says "whoever humbles himself will be exalted" in three settings: the choice of seats (Luk 14:11), the refusal of titles (Mat 23:12) and the two men at prayer (Luk 18:14); He gives it a face in the tax collector (Luk 18:13); He sets a child in the midst: "Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest" (Mat 18:4); He moves the disciples' joy from spirits being subject to them to "your names are written in heaven" (Luk 10:20).

What he taught happens to him. "he humbled himself … Therefore God has highly exalted him" (Phili 2:8–9). "made lower than the angels … crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death" (Heb 2:9). I read: the shape of the saying he taught (humbles himself, is exalted) is the shape told of him. Phili 2:9's "Therefore" joins his humbling to his exaltation. The tie back to the saying in Luke is mine.

He is the ground and the example for humility toward others. Phili 2:3–5 makes "in humility count others more significant" rest on "this mind … in Christ Jesus". Also 1Pe 2:21; Eph 5:21; 2Cor 10:1; Mat 11:29.

All things are put under him, and he is subject to the Father: "God has put all things in subjection under his feet" (1Cor 15:27; Eph 1:22; 1Pe 3:22; Heb 2:8); The bridge to the OT is in the text; Psa 8 says it of "man": "Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor … you have put all things under his feet" (Psa 8:5–6); Heb 2 quotes the psalm and reads it as "namely Jesus" (2:6–9). It adds: "At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him" (2:8–9); "Made lower" is H2637 in the psalm and G1642 in Hebrews, both T3; I read: the lowering said of man in Psa 8 is said of Jesus in Heb 2, and the subjection of all things to man is said of the Son. At the end, the Son "himself" is subjected to the Father (1Cor 15:28).

Others lower themselves before him: John the Baptist: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (Joh 3:30). G1642 is the same word as Jesus "made lower" in Heb 2:7, 9. Its setting: "I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him" (3:28), and "this joy of mine is now complete" (3:29); I read: John's lowering of himself before Jesus is said with joy, not loss.

At his coming, God looks on a low estate: Mary: "he has looked on the humble estate of his servant" (Luk 1:48), and "he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty" (1:52–53); I read: Mary's words stand with Hannah's: "he brings low and he exalts. He raises up the poor from the dust" (1Sa 2:7–8). The text does not quote Hannah.

OT: God "looks far down" and raises the poor (Psa 113:6–7); "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly" (Psa 138:6); he dwells with the contrite and lowly "to revive" (Isa 57:15); "your gentleness made me great" (2Sa 22:36; Psa 18:35); "I have been broken over their whoring heart" (Eze 6:9).

In the Son: in the form of God, "emptied himself … humbled himself … obedient to the point of death" (Phili 2:6–8); "gentle and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29); "made lower than the angels", crowned "because of the suffering of death" (Heb 2:9); "submissive to them" (Luk 2:51); "the Son himself will also be subjected" (1Cor 15:28); the humble king (Mat 21:5); his humiliation, silent (Act 8:32–33).

God's acts toward the humble and the proud (route A, already read): gives favor and grace (Pro 3:34; Jam 4:6); sees and answers the one who humbles himself (2Ch 12:7; 1Ki 21:29); humbles to test (Deu 8); brings the proud low (Isa 2; Psa 18:27; Dan 4:37); looks on a humble estate (Luk 1:48).
13.1 already holds Dan 4:17 and 4:37 (Willing), Psa 51:16–17 (Delight), Jam 4:4–6 (Jealousy) and Isa 58:3, 5 (Choosing). None is placed for God's lowering.

Words not pulled. Jesus' humility is also told without any lowering word: "the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve" (Mar 10:45; Mat 20:28); the washing of the disciples' feet (Joh 13); "though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor" (2Cor 8:9, which is in M09's poor/needy split, code S).

The serve and servant words were not in this fan-out. Phili 2:7 ("the form of a servant") shows they bear on it: Recommendation: a small surface pull of the serve/servant words in the Gospels and Phili 2, to see what they add to Jesus' part. It is not done here; The OT side was read only through the words pulled. "Bow down" (H7812) was left as a reading question (batch 1). It was not read.

Humbling oneself before God, and God's answer: OT: "When the Lord saw that they humbled themselves … I will not destroy them" (2Ch 12:7); Manasseh "humbled himself greatly … God was moved by his entreaty" (2Ch 33:12–13); "humbled yourself before your God, your words have been heard" (Dan 10:12); NT: the tax collector, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner!" and "this man went down to his house justified" (Luk 18:13–14); "Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you" (Jam 4:10); "under the mighty hand of God … casting all your anxieties on him" (1Pe 5:6–7).

The proud brought low, the humble raised: OT: "he brings low and he exalts" (1Sa 2:7); "One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor" (Pro 29:23); "Exalt that which is low, and bring low that which is exalted" (Eze 21:26); Isa 2:11, 17; NT: "he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate" (Luk 1:52); "Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted" (Mat 23:12; the same saying in Luk 14:11 and 18:14).

God gives favor to the humble (the NT quotes the OT): OT: "Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor" (Pro 3:34); NT: "Therefore it says, 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble'" (Jam 4:6; 1Pe 5:5).

Taking the lower place: OT: "better to be told, 'Come up here,' than to be put lower in the presence of a noble" (Pro 25:7); NT: "go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, 'Friend, move up higher'" (Luk 14:10).
The meek inherit: OT: "the meek shall inherit the land" (Psa 37:11); NT: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth" (Mat 5:5).

God humbles, for good: OT: "that he might humble you and test you, to do you good in the end" (Deu 8:16); NT: "he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness" (Heb 12:10); "be subject to the Father of spirits and live" (12:9).

A humbling God does not accept: OT: the fast with "your own pleasure": "Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?" (Isa 58:3); NT: "self-made religion and asceticism" that leaves one "puffed up" (Col 2:18, 23); the Pharisee's "I fast twice a week" (Luk 18:12).

Humility beside hearing the word: OT: "he who listens to reproof gains intelligence … humility comes before honor" (Pro 15:32–33); "humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word" (Isa 66:2); NT: "quick to hear, slow to speak … receive with meekness the implanted word" (Jam 1:19, 21).
The humble king (the NT quotes the OT): OT: "your king is coming to you … humble and mounted on a donkey" (Zec 9:9); NT: "This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet" (Mat 21:4–5).

God lowering himself: OT: "who looks far down on the heavens and the earth? He raises the poor" (Psa 113:6–7); "though the Lord is high, he regards the lowly" (Psa 138:6); "I dwell … also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (Isa 57:15); "your gentleness made me great" (2Sa 22:36); NT: "who, though he was in the form of God … emptied himself … humbled himself" (Phili 2:6–8); "I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29).
Mat 11:29: What it says of him: "I am gentle and lowly in heart", his own word on his heart.
Mat 21:5 (Zec 9:9): What it says of him: "your king is coming to you, humble".
Luk 2:51: What it says of him: "he went down with them … and was submissive to them", after "I must be in my Father's house" (2:49).
Act 8:33 (Isa 53): What it says of him: "In his humiliation justice was denied him", the lamb that "opens not his mouth" (8:32).

Phili 2:6–8: What it says of him: "though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant … he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross".
Heb 2:9: What it says of him: "him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus".
1Cor 15:28: What it says of him: "then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all".
